results.title: Byo to honour goalkeeping great Lucky Dube
results.description: Lovemore Dube lovemore.dube@chronicle.co.zw FORMER Zimbabwe national team goalkeeper Lucky Dube will be remembered next Saturday with a tombstone unveiling ceremony and a football tournament in Bulawayo as family, friends and the football fraternity celebrate the life of one of the country’s most gifted goalkeepers. Dube, who died in 1997 at the age of 34, would have turned 63 on Thursday last week. His widow, Mrs Sekani Dube (née Ntutu), confirmed that the family had organised a day of remembrance beginning with the unveiling of his tombstone in the morning before a social football tournament featuring four teams in Mzilikazi. “I am delighted that we will celebrate his life as family, my two sons with him and their four brothers. The children have come together to arrange the ceremony and we will have football because it was his love and it gave him fame and fortune,” she said. The tournament will feature Wolves of Nguboyenja, Madamara FC, Barbourfields Stars and Mzilikazi United, clubs chosen because Dube grew up in Mzilikazi and interacted closely with young footballers from neighbouring Nguboyenja. Born in Bulawayo, Dube attended Nhlambabaloyi Primary School before completing his Grade Seven education at Mzilikazi High School. He began his football career at Highlanders juniors before joining Bulawayo Wanderers, where his talent quickly became evident. By 1980, he had earned selection into Zimbabwe’s pioneering Under-20 national team shortly after Independence. His performances later earned him a move to Bata Power before joining Dynamos, where he replaced Japhet Mparutsa after the latter moved to Black Rhinos in 1983. During his successful stay in Harare, Dube won several trophies with the Glamour Boys before returning to Bulawayo in 1989. Mrs Dube recalled how she was introduced to football through him. “One day around 1980 when I was still at school, he asked me to accompany him to a football match. My brother Felix played football but I did not care much about the sport. I agreed to accompany him and we found curtain-raisers in action. I did not know Lucky Dube was a football player. “After watching for a while, he excused himself and said he would be back shortly. My jaw dropped when I saw him in football gear starting for Bulawayo Wanderers. The rest is history. He gave me two wonderful sons, Thabo and Nhlanhla. He was a loving man, very sociable and quite smart,” she said. Both sons followed their father into football. Nhlanhla played for Highlanders and Zimbabwe Saints, while Thabo graduated from Rutz Celtics juniors into the club’s Division Two side that later won promotion to Division One. Thabo said growing up as the son of a football legend came with enormous expectations. “I think I speak for all my siblings when I say growing up as a legend’s son was not easy because people expected the same or even better from us. He always reminded us that we had big shoes to fill. “Our father was a legend, the smartest man I have ever known. He was punctual, disciplined and always encouraged us to think outside the box,” he said. Dynamos chairman Vincent Chawonza described Dube as one of the club’s outstanding servants. “Without doubt he is a Dynamos legend and he won a lot with the club. He will always remain in our hearts and Dynamos will participate in the day chosen by his family to remember him,” said Chawonza. Former national team goalkeeper Japhet Mparutsa, who competed with Dube for places in the Under-20 side, recently paid tribute to him on social media. “Lucky Dube was our first-choice goalkeeper. He was tall, gifted, confident and naturally talented. He carried himself with professionalism and pride,” wrote Mparutsa. He said competing with Dube pushed him to improve his own game. “I respected Lucky because he was talented, but I also believed in my own ability and wanted to keep improving. Competing with a talented goalkeeper like him pushed me to become better,” he wrote. Mparutsa would later become the first goalkeeper to win the Soccer Star of the Year award in 1982. Dube and Mparutsa were part of a generation of goalkeepers that included Frank Mkanga, Victor Dliwayo, Posani Sibanda, Mike Mhlanga, Stewart Gilbert, Raphael Phiri, Labani Kandi and Peter Nkomo. Nearly three decades after his death, Dube remains fondly remembered by family, former teammates, supporters and football historians as a talented goalkeeper whose elegance, intelligence and professionalism left a lasting mark on Zimbabwean football.

results.title: Saving vultures through art: Byo creatives answer nature’s call
results.description: Mbulelo Mpofu Sunday Life Reporter THE often-maligned vulture is set to become the unlikely muse for Zimbabwe’s next generation of artists as conservationists turn to creativity to change public perceptions of one of nature’s most misunderstood birds. In commemoration of International Vulture Awareness Day (IVAD) 2026, celebrated annually on the first Saturday of September, BirdLife Zimbabwe’s Matabeleland Branch Committee and the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe have launched an open call inviting artists aged 35 years and below to explore and express the vital ecological role of vultures through visual art under the theme, “Vulture Interactions”. The exhibition will form part of commemorations to be held at the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe in Bulawayo on September 6, bringing together conservationists, artists, young people and members of the public in a united effort to spotlight a species facing an increasingly uncertain future. Paintings, drawings, photos, digital art, mixed media and installations will dress the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe in Bulawayo walls. One of the leaders of the initiative, Mthabisi Bafana Charles Khumalo, curator of the Ornithology Department at the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe and Special Species and Raptors Coordinator for BirdLife Zimbabwe’s Matabeleland Branch Committee, who believes art can become a powerful conservation tool. IVAD has grown into a global campaign dedicated to highlighting the ecological importance of vultures while drawing attention to the urgent need for their protection. The campaign was established to challenge long-held misconceptions surrounding vultures, birds that are frequently associated with death and decay despite playing a critical role in maintaining healthy ecosystems. The first co-ordinated global observance was launched in 2009 by the Hawk Conservancy Trust in the United Kingdom and the Endangered Wildlife Trust in South Africa. Since then, conservation organisations around the world have used the occasion to educate communities, influence policy and promote rescue and rehabilitation initiatives. This year’s Bulawayo commemorations seek to build on that legacy by merging conservation with artistic expression. “Our plan is to drive vulture conservation impact by spreading awareness through a commemoration at the Natural History Museum and an art exhibition with the theme ‘Vulture Interactions’. We want to use the power of art by engaging young creatives (35 years and below) to exhibit their vulture art and inspire the audience in conservation, fulfilling a crucial need to involve youth and shift public perception. “It is a perfect blend of education and community engagement, which is essential for driving behavioural and societal change,” said Khumalo. The initiative comes against the backdrop of an alarming decline in Zimbabwe’s vulture populations. Of the 11 vulture species found across Africa, six occur in Zimbabwe, with all but one listed as threatened or endangered. Among the most imperilled are the white-backed vulture, white-headed vulture and hooded vulture, all of which are classified as Critically Endangered. Conservationists warn that the disappearance of these scavengers would have devastating consequences not only for biodiversity, but also for public health and the economy. Poisoning remains the single greatest threat. Poachers frequently lace animal carcasses with poison to eliminate vultures whose circling flight patterns can expose illegal hunting activities to wildlife authorities. These incidents often result in catastrophic losses, including the poisoning of 191 vultures in Gonarezhou National Park in 2012 and another 94 birds near the park’s boundary in 2017. Accidental poisonings are also widespread, particularly in farming communities where poisoned carcasses intended to kill predators such as lions and hyenas are later consumed by vultures. Another major challenge is belief-based use, where vultures are killed for body parts believed to possess supernatural powers for use in traditional medicine. Across Africa, this practice accounts for an estimated 27 percent of threats facing vultures. To address the issue, BirdLife Zimbabwe has partnered with the Zimbabwe National Traditional Healers’ Association (Zinatha), whose members have pledged to identify sustainable alternatives to the use of vulture parts in traditional healing practices. Habitat destruction presents another growing concern. Illegal farming and land-use changes continue to reduce nesting and feeding habitats, while a 2025 Nasa study highlighted the impact of drought and elephant damage on vegetation surrounding waterholes, threatening the nesting trees used by white-backed vultures. Electrocutions and collisions with power lines further compound the pressures facing already declining populations. Despite their often negative reputation, vultures perform one of nature’s most essential ecological services. Often referred to as nature’s clean-up crew, they rapidly dispose of animal carcasses before they become breeding grounds for dangerous diseases. Their uniquely acidic digestive systems enable them to consume pathogens such as anthrax and rabies without becoming infected, effectively preventing the spread of diseases to livestock, wildlife and people. The economic contribution of this natural sanitation service is equally remarkable. Studies estimate that vultures save Zimbabwe more than US$1 million annually through free waste disposal services that would otherwise require costly human intervention. A former Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority (ZimParks) director once estimated that a single vulture provides ecosystem services worth more than US$11 000 during its lifetime. International research has also illustrated the consequences of vulture declines. In India, the collapse of vulture populations triggered an explosion in feral dog numbers and contributed to tens of thousands of additional rabies-related deaths. Researchers are now investigating whether Zimbabwe’s recent anthrax outbreaks may similarly be linked to declining vulture populations. Khumalo believes the Bulawayo commemorations represent an important contribution to Zimbabwe’s broader conservation strategy. “Our event directly supports the long-term survival of these critically important birds by educating the public, engaging the next generation of conservationists, and celebrating the misunderstood, yet essential, vulture,” he said. The programme brings together BirdLife Zimbabwe’s Matabeleland Branch, the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe’s Ornithology Department and the Conservation Sisters Connect programme under Wildlife Conservation Action. The partnership seeks to combine scientific expertise, youth engagement and artistic expression while strengthening conservation leadership among young Zimbabweans, particularly women. Conservation Sisters Connect is a fellowship programme that equips young women with practical conservation skills and mentorship, helping build a stronger future generation of environmental leaders. The commemorations also complement BirdLife Zimbabwe’s wider conservation efforts under the Zimbabwe Vulture Action Plan, developed jointly with ZimParks and other stakeholders. As the lead co-ordinator of the national strategy, BirdLife Zimbabwe oversees the Vulture Working Group, which brings together government agencies, researchers and non-governmental organisations to coordinate conservation interventions. Its work ranges from establishing Vulture Safe Zones and community-based Vulture Support Groups to deploying satellite tracking technology, in partnership with IFAW and ZimParks, to monitor bird movements and identify poaching hotspots. The organisation also continues advocating for stronger wildlife protection laws while expanding community education programmes across the country. By inviting young artists to interpret the theme, “Vulture Interactions”, organisers hope creativity will become a catalyst for changing attitudes towards birds that have for generations been unfairly associated with superstition and death. Instead, the exhibition seeks to present vultures for what they truly are - silent custodians of ecosystem health whose survival is inseparable from that of Zimbabwe’s wildlife, landscapes and communities. IVAD approaches, conservationists are hopeful that brushes, canvases and imagination will succeed where fear and misunderstanding have long prevailed, giving Zimbabwe’s embattled vultures a renewed voice through the language of art. – Follow on X @MbuleloMpofu

results.title: 20-year health masterplan to transform health sector
results.description: Nqobile Bhebhe Zimpapers Senior Reporter GOVERNMENT will next year embark on the development of a comprehensive 20-Year Health Infrastructure Master Plan designed to transform Zimbabwe’s healthcare delivery system through data-driven planning, strategic investment and expanded access to quality medical services. Presenting the 2026 Mid-Term Budget Review in Parliament, Finance, Economic Development and Investment Promotion Minister Professor Mthuli Ncube said the long-term infrastructure strategy would culminate in the development of a national health infrastructure blueprint to guide investment over the next two decades. “Government will also develop a 20-Year Health Infrastructure Master Plan, incorporating GIS based infrastructure mapping, population and service demand projections and investment case development,” he said. The proposed master plan is expected to strengthen evidence-based decision-making, improve coordination of health infrastructure investments and position Zimbabwe to meet future healthcare needs through a modern, resilient and sustainable public health system. Prof Ncube said the health sector will remain a key priority in the 2027 National Budget, with increased investment targeting service delivery, infrastructure development and sustainable healthcare financing. “Health Services Priority will be accorded to strengthening primary healthcare, reducing maternal and child mortality and expanding access to essential medicines. Resources will be channeled towards community health programmes, disease surveillance and pharmaceutical security, complemented by scaled-up domestic health financing to progressively reduce donor dependency and advance universal health coverage,” he said. He said expanding and modernising healthcare infrastructure will be central to improving access to quality medical services across Zimbabwe. “Alongside service delivery, the Government will expand and modernise health infrastructure to improve access, quality, resilience and safety of health services countrywide. In 2027, infrastructure investment will centre on the construction of primary and secondary care facilities in underserved communities, targeting completion and equipment of Manyame Hospital, Lupane and Masvingo Provincial Hospitals new primary care facilities, urban district hospitals in Harare and Bulawayo, the upgrading of provincial and tertiary hospitals and staff accommodation at selected facilities,” he added. The planned investments underscore Government’s commitment to reducing geographical disparities in healthcare access by expanding services to previously underserved communities while upgrading existing institutions to meet growing demand. The long-term blueprint, which will incorporate Geographic Information Systems (GIS)-based infrastructure mapping, population growth projections, health service demand forecasting and investment case development, forms part of the Government’s broader strategy to build a resilient, equitable and modern health sector. The proposed master plan is expected to provide the Government with a scientific framework for planning future health infrastructure, ensuring that investments are aligned with demographic changes, disease burden and regional healthcare needs while addressing infrastructure gaps across the country. In addition, the strategy seeks to improve the efficiency of public health spending and support Zimbabwe’s drive towards Universal Health Coverage. Prof Ncube said the Government will continue strengthening healthcare services by prioritising preventive and community-based interventions while reducing dependence on external funding. The programme also seeks to improve working conditions for healthcare professionals through the construction of staff accommodation, a move expected to enhance staff retention, particularly in remote areas. Prof Ncube said the health infrastructure programme would also focus on rehabilitating existing facilities to improve service quality and patient safety. “Government will also target the refurbishment and upgrading of central, provincial and district hospitals, including theatres, wards, outpatient departments, kitchens, laundries, mortuaries and incinerators, across provinces and districts,” he said. Recognising the growing impact of climate-related shocks and utility disruptions on healthcare delivery, the Government will also invest in renewable energy and water security for health institutions. “To enhance resilience to utility disruptions, priority will also be accorded to the solarisation of public health facilities and staff accommodation, alongside the installation of boreholes and water storage systems,” he said.
